title: From SUVs to Silver Bars, Companies Go Big on Diwali Gifts in 2026
excerpt: A Panchkula pharmaceutical company gave four Kia Sonet SUVs to its top performers and opened a lucky draw for the rest of its staff, while silver bars and premium hampers led the wider corporate gifting season.
body:
• MITS Healthcare in Panchkula gave four brand-new Kia Sonet SUVs to its top-performing employees this Diwali, continuing a tradition its founder MK Bhatia began four years ago.
  • The company added a lucky draw this year: staff with at least 18 months of service — from security guards to senior officials — were entered, with 35 people in the draw held on October 28.
  • Across the wider corporate season, premium gifts ran from hallmarked silver bars and gold gift cards to smartwatches, fragrances and customised watches, according to Titan's corporate gifting guide.
  • Silver bars sit in the premium band of that guide, pitched at long-serving employees, executives and high-value business partners.

Most workplace Diwali gifts stop at bonuses and hampers. At MITS Healthcare in Panchkula, the festive reward is a car. The pharmaceutical company gave four brand-new Kia Sonet SUVs to its top performers this year, continuing a practice founder and chairman MK Bhatia started four years ago, The Daily Jagran reported. The company shared videos of the recipients unveiling their vehicles at a dealership.

A draw for everyone else

The new element in 2026 is breadth. Alongside the performance awards, MITS opened a lucky draw for employees who have completed at least 18 months of service, across every level of the organisation. One car was announced for the draw, which was scheduled for October 28 with 35 people included. The structure matters: a performance-only scheme rewards a handful of people, while the draw gives the rest of the workforce a stake in the celebration.

Silver at the premium end

Cars are the extreme end of a season that has moved steadily upmarket. Titan's corporate gifting guide for 2026 lists silver bars among its popular premium options, alongside customised watches, Tanishq gift cards, fragrances and smartwatches. It describes engraved silver bars — carrying a message or company logo — as holding both intrinsic monetary value and symbolic value, and places hallmarked silver bars in its premium budget band of Rs 3,000 to Rs 10,000 and above, aimed at long-serving employees, executive leadership and high-value partners.

The logic is consistent across both ends of the scale. A hamper is consumed and forgotten; a silver bar is kept, and a car is driven to work every day. In a tight hiring market, companies are treating the Diwali gift less as a ritual and more as a retention statement — one that, in Panchkula, now comes with keys.

How the budgets break down

Titan's guide sorts the season into three bands. Entry-level gifts under Rs 1,000 run to desk planters, snack boxes and accessories. The mid-range band, Rs 1,000 to Rs 3,000, covers fragrance sets, smartwatches and digital vouchers. The premium band above Rs 3,000 is where the watches, gold and silver gift cards and hallmarked silver bars sit — the tier aimed at leadership, long-serving staff and key clients. Personalisation is the common thread the guide pushes at every level: engraving, branding and a named message are what separate a kept gift from a regifted one. Read against the MITS example, the pattern is clear — employers are spending more per person on fewer, more durable symbols, and the festival's association with prosperity makes precious metal and, at the extreme, a vehicle feel on-theme rather than extravagant.
